title: 思いやり予算 5年3兆円超を米要求
body:
2027年度から5年間の在日米軍駐留経費負担（思いやり予算）を巡り、トランプ米政権が現行の3倍程度となる3兆円超を日本政府に要求したことが分かった。日本側は要求通りには応じないものの、現行水準から大幅に増額して1兆5千億円程度にする検討に入った。米軍基地が攻撃されても被害を極小化する防護強化費用を盛り込む見通しで、単年度当たり3千億円超となる可能性がある。年内合意を目指して来週にも詰めの協議に入る。複数の関係者が12日、明らかにした。【写真】ビル・ゲイツ氏が暴露したトランプ氏の「無知さ」　18年記事
日米外交筋は「5年で3兆円は受け入れがたいが、1兆5千億円程度になる可能性はある」と語った。現行の22～26年度分の駐留経費負担は総額1兆551億円で合意。単年度当たりでは約2110億円となる。過去最大の負担額は1996～2000年度の計1兆3521億円だった。日米両政府は今夏に東京で交渉を本格化させた。10月上旬に米国、下旬には日本で実務者協議を実施した。思いやり予算は、トランプ大統領が第1次政権でも日本に巨額の負担を求めた経緯がある。

title: 参議院議員の山崎正昭氏が死去
body:
福井県大野市出身の参議院議員山崎正昭氏が13日未明、亡くなりました。現職の参議院議員では最高齢の84歳でした。【動画を見る】2022年参院選・山崎正昭氏（80）6度目の当選　喜びの声
山崎氏は日本大学法学部を卒業後、県議会議員などを務め1992年に参議院議員に初当選しました。以降、内閣官房副長官などの要職を経て、2013年には県選出の国会議員では初となる参議院議長に選出されました。2022年には6期目となる当選を果たしていました。

title: Microsoft障害 全面復旧は未定
body: アメリカのIT大手｢マイクロソフト｣は、メールサービスなどで世界的に広がっている障害について、｢限定的な復旧がみられる｣と発表しました。【速報中】マイクロソフトで大規模通信障害 情報まとめ日本時間13日未明から企業向けクラウドサービス｢マイクロソフト365｣で障害が発生し、メールソフトの｢Outlook｣などに接続できない状態が続いています。マイクロソフトは、多数のサーバーが予期せずに停止し、残りのサーバーに負荷が集中していると説明しています。停止したサーバーの一部を順次復旧させて、安定した状態を維持していると発表していました。しかしその後マイクロソフトは、利用者からの通信を受けると再び応答しなくなる場合があると明らかにしました。原因は分析中で、一部の地域で一時的に通信を制限したり、サーバーを以前の設定で作り直したりして、再発を防げるか検証しているということです。大規模障害の根本的な原因はいまだ判明しておらず、復旧の見通しもたっていません。

title: メルセデス 独工場の一部閉鎖検討
body: Ilona Wissenbach[フランクフルト １２日 ロイター] - ドイツ自動車大手メルセデス・ベンツは、ド‌イツ国内における自動車製造の高コ⁠ストに対処するため、国内工場への全ての投資を凍結し、一部の工場を閉鎖​することを検討している。ロイターが入手した１２日付の社内メモで明‌らかになった。ドイツの自動車業界の危機がさらに深刻化している事態を浮‌き彫りにする動き‌だ。社内イントラネットに掲載​された経営陣へのインタビューで、経営陣と労働‌組合代表との間で人件費削減について合意に至らなか‌ったため、投資凍​結を決定したことが明らかになった。メ‌ルセデスは従業員に対し、コスト削減策の検討を⁠強く求めてきた。生産責任者のミヒャエル・シーベ氏は９月に、この問題で進展が見られない場合、⁠国内の２工場が閉鎖される可​能性があると‌警告していた。メモの内容は、経営陣が現時点で閉鎖の可能性に備えていることを示唆してい⁠る。メモでブリッタ・ゼーガー取締⁠役は「何としても工場の閉鎖を避けたい。しかし⁠残念だが、今やこの選択肢をより詳細に検討せざるを‌得な⁠い」と述べた。こうした脅威が浮上する​中、ドイツ最大の労組であるＩＧメタルとの交渉は続いている。

title: 奈良で妻が行方不明 捜索続け12年
body:
12年前に奈良市で観光中に行方不明となった妻、林まゆみさん(当時56)を捜索している山口県周南市の林洋二さん(74)が10日、奈良新聞社を訪れ、情報の提供を呼びかけた。[写真]行方不明となった妻まゆみさんの情報提供を呼びかける林洋二さん=10日、奈良市法華寺町の奈良新聞社
林さん夫妻は2014年11月1日、バスツアーで奈良を訪問。奈良市の若草山麓で昼食後、洋二さんは土産物を買うため「先にバスに乗っておいて」と声をかけてまゆみさんと一時離れ、買い物後にバスに戻ったところまゆみさんの姿がなかった。その後、携帯電話の位置情報からまゆみさんは斑鳩町の町立斑鳩東小学校周辺にいることが判明。洋二さんは警察官と共に捜したが見つからず消息を絶った。ツアーでは若草山麓の次の目的地が同町の法隆寺だった。当時、まゆみさんは若年性認知症の傾向があったという。洋二さんは県警と連携しながら捜索を続けており、「12年がたち区切りをつけないといけないと思っており、奈良に来るのも最後になるかもしれない。情報があればご連絡いただきたい」と訴えた。情報提供は奈良署生活安全課、電話0742(20)0110。

title: 米首都銃撃5人死傷 容疑者も死亡
body:
【ワシントン共同】米首都ワシントン中心部のジムで12日朝、銃撃事件が発生し、警察幹部は1人が死亡、4人が負傷したと明らかにした。容疑者は建物内に立てこもった後、自らを撃ったという。複数の米メディアによると、容疑者は死亡した。【写真】米国各地で銃撃、24人死亡　ハロウィーン前後、NYタイムズ
現場はローガン・サークルと呼ばれる地区で、ホワイトハウスから北東に約1.6キロの距離。警察は現場一帯を封鎖し、市民に近づかないよう求めた。在米日本大使館も注意喚起のメールを在留邦人に送った。

title: 米NYで建物崩壊8人死亡 17人負傷
body: 【ニューヨーク時事】米ニューヨーク市ブルックリンの住宅街で11日、3階建てのビルが崩壊し、8人が死亡し、少なくとも17人が負傷した。【写真特集】「危険」が発生中建物が崩れた経緯は不明だが、隣接する建設現場ではこの日、掘削作業が行われていた。市消防局は現地時間11日午後4時ごろに通報を受けた。がれきに閉じ込められた人の救出活動が、一夜明けた12日も続いている。

title: 露ウ 大規模な捕虜交換で合意
body: ロシアによるウクライナ侵略の終結に向けた米露ウクライナ3カ国の高官協議は11日、アラブ首長国連邦（UAE）の首都アブダビで2日間の日程を終えた。露代表団のメジンスキー大統領補佐官は11日、協議終了後に記者会見し、露ウクライナが大規模な捕虜交換で合意したと発表した。ロシアの占領下にあるウクライナ領の扱いなど重要問題で進展があったかどうかは明言しなかった。一方、ウィットコフ米和平交渉担当特使とともに協議に参加したトランプ米大統領の娘婿クシュナー氏は協議後、ウィットコフ氏と露首都モスクワを12日に訪問してプーチン露大統領と会談し、アブダビでの協議の結果について話し合うと明らかにした。露国営タス通信が伝えた。（小野田雄一）

title: 駐米ロシア大使が死去 疾患が原因
body: ロシア外務省は11日、アレクサンドル・ダルチエフ駐米大使が同日死亡したと発表した。66歳だった。「急逝」としているが、ロシア外務省のザハロワ報道官は「慢性疾患」が原因だとSNSで明らかにした。ダルチエフ氏は駐カナダ大使や北大西洋局長などを経て、2025年3月から駐米大使を務めていた。【写真】満足げなプーチン氏と口数が減ったトランプ氏　米ロ会談の「勝者」はロシアメディアによると、ダルチエフ氏は1983年にモスクワ大学を卒業。92年にロシア外務省に入り、主に北米関連の部門を歴任した。トランプ米大統領の2期目の就任後、ウクライナ全面侵攻後に途絶えていた米ロの本格的な協議が再開されると、2025年2月からイスタンブールで開かれた米ロ協議でロシア代表団を率いた。

title: 米有権者 党派対立にも警戒感
body:
中間選挙直後に米国で行われたロイターとイプソスの共同世論調査の結果が11月10日、発表された。
それによると71%（共和党支持者だけでも51%）は「イラン戦争を終わらせる法律を議会が作ることに賛成」と回答し、この戦争の不人気ぶりが改めて浮き彫りになった。
その一方で「トランプ弾劾がよいこと」と回答したのは33%（民主党支持者だけだと63%だが、有権者の約4割を占める無党派層では30%）にとどまった。
つまり米国ではイラン戦争に辟易している有権者が多いものの、トランプ政権を追い詰めることにも慎重な姿勢も目立つ。
Americans also express a desire for cooperation （後略）出典：Ipsos　2026/11/10(火)
一方、選挙で大勝した民主党はトランプ一族に対する腐敗追及の動きを強めるなど攻防が激しくなっている。出典：テレビ朝日系（ANN）　2026/11/11(水)
トランプ米大統領は（中略）大統領執務室の机上に「VETO（拒否権）」と書かれた赤い帽子を置き、記者団の取材に応じた。出典：産経新聞：産経ニュース　2026/11/6(金)
手法は異なるがギャロップの調査でも45%が「独立系」と回答している。出典：六辻彰二　2026/11/6(金)
ロイターとイプソスの調査で、「議会は物価対策に重点を置くべき」に賛成が「大いに」と「やや」を含めて78%（共和党支持者でも70%）など、生活改善の要望が目立ったのは大方の予想通りといえる。
その一方で注目すべきは「トランプが議会民主党と協力すること」を「重要」と回答したのが81%（共和党支持者でも87%）、「議会民主党がトランプと協力すること」を「重要」と回答したのが74%（民主党支持者でも69%）だったことだ。
つまり有権者の多くはイラン戦争がもたらした生活悪化への不満が大きい反面、党派対立にも警戒感が強い。
民主党ではトランプ政権に対する弾劾や調査を進めるべきという声が強く、これに対してトランプは民主党中心の議会の法案に逐一拒否権を発動すると示唆しているが、国民生活の改善に直結しない点ではどちらも共通するからだ。
むしろ有権者の多くは政治的立場を超えた協力による難局克服を望んでいるといえる。
トランプ登場の前後から米国では分断が深刻化してきたが、この世論調査からはイデオロギー対立に疲れた米国人の間に中庸を求める傾向が強くなっていることがうかがえる。ただし一般米国人のこの良識が政治家にどこまで届くかは未知数だ。

title: エヌビディアCEO辞任 動揺広がる
body: 中国の工作員とされる女性との不倫関係が問題となった半導体大手エヌビディアのフアンCEOが辞任したことを受け、アメリカ国内では動揺が広がっています。【写真を見る】フアンCEOの隣に座る女性…中国スパイか フアン氏は不倫認める記者「エヌビディアの本社前です。従業員が警備員に守られながら足早に出勤していきます」創業者のフアンCEOの辞任を発表したエヌビディアの本社では、朝から厳戒態勢が敷かれました。AIブームをけん引してきた世界的経営者に不倫問題が浮上し、その後、辞任したことに、本社があるカリフォルニア州のシリコンバレーでも動揺が広がっています。「非常に大きなニュース。スパイ疑惑や情報漏えいについて、何が本当で何がうそなのか、CEO交代後のエヌビディアがどうなるのか関心がある」「ビジネス面では、素晴らしいリーダーだと思う」「（不倫は）個人的な問題。あまりコメントすべきではない」辞任を受け、12日のニューヨーク株式市場では、取引開始と同時にエヌビディアの株価が大きく値を下げ、一時、前日の終値から14％以上も安い、148ドル80セントまで急落しました。こうしたなか、ブルームバーグ通信など複数のアメリカメディアは、フアン氏が近く連邦議会の聴取に応じる意向を示していると報じました。証言は来週以降に非公開で行われる見通しで、現在、日程調整が進められているということです。議会では、今回の問題へのトランプ政権の対応に批判が強まっていて、野党だけでなく与党議員からも、半導体輸出の規制を担当するラトニック商務長官の議会証言を求める声があがっています。

title: エヌビディアのフアンCEOが辞任
body: アメリカの半導体大手エヌビディアは、さきほど、創業者のジェンスン・フアンCEOが辞任したと発表しました。【写真を見る】フアンCEOの隣に座る女性…中国スパイか フアン氏は不倫認めるフアン氏は社長と取締役も退任し、後任が決まるまで、最高財務責任者のコレット・クレス氏が暫定的にCEOを務めます。フアン氏をめぐっては、中国の情報機関との関係が疑われる女性との不倫関係が報じられ、会社の取締役会が調査を進めていました。今回の発表では、辞任の理由は明らかにされていません。フアン氏は1993年にエヌビディアを創業し、AI向け半導体で世界をリードする企業に成長させました。

title: タマホーム 5年以上前から不正か
body: 住宅メーカー・タマホームが損害保険会社に対して火災保険の不正請求をしていた疑いについて、少なくとも5年以上前から不正請求が行われていた可能性があることが関係者への取材でわかりました。【画像】少なくとも200件以上…数千万円規模か　タマホームが火災保険金“不正請求”この問題は、タマホーム高松支店の複数の社員が損害保険会社に対して火災保険の不正請求を行っていた疑いがあるものです。不正はことし4月頃に確認されたということですが、関係者への取材で、少なくとも5年以上前から不正請求が行われていた可能性があることがわかりました。過去の火災や事故の写真を使い回して別の保険金の請求をするなどしたとみられ、不正は少なくともあわせて200件以上、数千万円規模にのぼるとみられています。タマホームは「多大なるご迷惑とご心配をおかけしておりますこと、深くお詫び申し上げます。現在、事実関係および全容解明に向けた調査を鋭意進めております。事実関係の確認が取れ次第、速やかに適切な形でご報告させていただく所存です」とコメントしています。

title: Scandal-hit Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang quits, plunging AI chipmaking giant into turmoil
summary: US lawmakers now want to question him over whether one of his alleged relationships was with a Chinese spy.
body:
Watch: What we know so far about Nvidia CEO resignation
Jensen Huang has abruptly quit as chief executive of AI chipmaking giant Nvidia after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, in a stunning fall from grace that sent shockwaves from Silicon Valley to Capitol Hill.
Nvidia is now under scrutiny from US lawmakers in Washington DC demanding Huang answer questions over whether one of his alleged relationships was with a Chinese spy.
One of the world's most valuable companies as a result of the AI boom, Nvidia has lost $550bn (£415bn) in stock market value in just five days as the scandal dominated headlines.
Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress, called an emergency meeting of her executive team to discuss the company's future.
His alleged conduct not only potentially crossed professional boundaries, but has made Nvidia the target of questions from US politicians who have expressed concern about national security risks.
Huang, who has been Nvidia's public face since 1993,admitted on Sunday to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang.
On Wednesday, he was reported to have had a second relationship, this time with an Nvidia executive.
Alice Huang (no relation) worked as an executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed. She has been suspected of being an intelligence asset for China, according to the New York Times. China has rejected that allegation as a smear.
And US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday the Department of Justice had not yet drawn any conclusions about whether Alice Huang was engaged in espionage for Beijing.
Senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons, along with other Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, publicly demanded that Huang brief Congress on the matter.
If he refuses to appear voluntarily before any committee that calls him, he could be subpoenaed, one Senate staff member told the BBC.
Nvidia officials have repeatedly declined to comment since Wednesday. A personal representative of Huang also declined to comment on Thursday.
According to US media, Huang's alleged second affair was with a long-time Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him within the company.
Sources have told the BBC that Nvidia employees had noticed the pair were unusually close.
Huang had been widely expected to weather the storm after the first affair became public, even as Nvidia announced it had launched an investigation into whether its CEO had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort".
One current Nvidia staff member told the BBC that the initial reports of his infidelity were more or less brushed off by rank-and-file workers inside the company.
It wasn't until Huang's alleged affair with the Nvidia executive became public that workers started to feel "this is crazy", the person said.
Another Nvidia employee said they had been told not to speak with the press or otherwise comment on the situation in public.
Many staff have earned millions of dollars in compensation through their ability to cash out their Nvidia shares as the stock soared.
Nvidia has said it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised", but pledged that its independent inquiry would look at all available information.
The company's meteoric rise had been led by Jensen Huang, who became a major booster of the AI industry, which relies on Nvidia for the powerful computer chips it manufactures.
Initially those chips were designed for computer gaming.
But as AI technology evolved in the last four years into chatbots and large language models, companies building AI tools suddenly required huge numbers of the Nvidia computer chips that could process large amounts of data.
Nvidia is now hunting a permanent replacement for Huang. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named on Thursday as interim CEO.
Several tech insiders that the BBC spoke with this week noted that Huang's downfall has been a major topic of conversation in San Francisco Bay area circles, an area filled with tech employees, industry executives and billionaires.
He is far from the first tech titan to become embroiled in revelations of infidelity.
Bill Gates of Microsoft and Jeff Bezos of Amazon had affairs exposed in the last decade. Both men are now divorced from their wives.
Huang has been married to Lori Huang for 40 years. Both of their children are also executives at Nvidia.
Nvidia's stock fall this week is the most significant five-day drop the company has seen since going public 27 years ago.
Its market value rose by more than 470% in the past five years, peaking just a few weeks ago. It is now down by 31% against a backdrop of wider uncertainty in the tech sector.
Because of Nvidia's size and success in recent years, such a drop can have a direct impact on the savings accounts of ordinary Americans.
Nvidia's value makes up about 7% of the S&P 500 index. That index is offered as a popular index fund in US retirement savings accounts.
Those account balances rise and fall with the changes of the stock market.

title: Zelensky welcomes US bringing Europe into Russia-Ukraine peace talks
summary: The Ukrainian president says it makes sense for European leaders to be involved as Ukraine hopes to eventually join the EU.
body:
US envoys Jared Kushner (left) and Steve Witkoff (right) met Volodymyr Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday evening
Ukraine's president has welcomed a pledge from US envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, to include delegates from the European Union in the next round of peace talks with Russia.
European leaders have expressed deepening security concerns this week, and Volodymyr Zelensky said bringing them into the talks would ensure the EU has a "voice" in negotiations.
Kushner and Witkoff met Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday evening as part of a busy day of shuttle diplomacy - they met Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier, who said that Russia's position on the war - and its demand for territory - has not changed.
The meetings follow talks in Abu Dhabi last week that failed to reach a breakthrough in ending the war.
But Thursday did see Russia and Ukraine agree to another prisoner exchange - the largest swap yet since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Kushner said it would return "thousands of people to their families", but further details like how many prisoners would be exchanged or a timeline, were not given.
US envoys meet Zelensky in Dublin after talks with Putin in Moscow
Europe's security 'fundamentally reshaped' by war in Ukraine
Zelensky has for several years been calling for European delegates to be included in the peace talks, and says it makes sense because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the European Union.
On Thursday, Kushner said that the US has been "working very, very closely over the past several months with Europeans and I think that that's been very important."
He added that he had stressed to Putin how important it is to have European delegates "at the table".
"He's willing to give it a try," Kushner added.
Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US government's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.
Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.
Earlier on Thursday, Vice President of the European Commission Kaja Kallas, the EU's top diplomat, told BBC's Newshour the presence of a European delegate showed the Kremlin "now realised that Europe is a big player".
Kallas also expressed doubts that there was Russian momentum towards a peace deal.
Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin told a host of Euro leaders gathered in the Irish capital on Thursday that he believed the security of the region has been "fundamentally reshaped" by Russia's war.
"Many member states [of the EU] feel an existential threat because of what has happened in Ukraine and the potential, if Ukraine was to fall, for further aggression on the European continent," he told reporters.
Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine remains under control of Russian forces, and cross-border incursions are increasingly common.
Tensions between the US and Ukraine were on display on Thursday before Witkoff and Kushner's meeting with Zelensky.
Earlier, the Ukrainian leader said that the military was facing more "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade satellite service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.
The technology owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company has played a vital role in government and military connectivity in Ukraine, and increasingly assists infacilitating communication on Ukraine's front line.

title: Neither war nor peace in Tigray - is Ethiopia's latest conflict really over?
summary: The army has taken control of most of Tigray's main towns - it is unclear if the TPLF is capable of fighting back.
body:
Pro-government forces marched into Tigray's capital less than two weeks after the war began
Running a hair salon in Mekelle, capital of Ethiopia's troubled northern Tigray region, is not easy at the moment.
"People can't prioritise beauty over daily basic needs. For many residents, thinking about self-care is a luxury, at a time when they can't feed their kids," Firut Me'ar, who runs a salon in the city, tells the BBC.
After a brief war, the city is under the control of the national army but life is far from normal, says Firut, a single mother of a 10-year-old daughter.
"Things are better than during the war, but people still have no money, no morale. Business is almost non-existent," she says, her voice shaking with emotion.
Above all, she says people are worried about what the future holds. "There is uncertainty about what comes next."
Fighting broke out in late September between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that had run Tigray for decades, and the national army - a resumption of the two-year civil war that officially ended in 2022.
But within less than two weeks, federal forces marched triumphantly into Mekelle. The TPLF made what it called a "strategic withdrawal" from the city and Tigray's other main towns so the army encountered little resistance. Hundreds of people are reported to have died in the conflict, including dozens killed by drone strikes and bombing raids by the air force.
Ethiopian government officials and supporters argue that the war is effectively over and that the only remaining task is to clear Tigray of TPLF elements.
Getachew Reda, a senior TPLF official who switched sides and is now an adviser to the prime minister, declared that the war in Tigray had ended and that stabilising the region should now be the immediate priority.
Cameroon Hudson, an analyst and consultant on African peace and security, says there are various reasons for the TPLF's rapid defeat.
"The TPLF has lost popular support at home. It is fragmented, it does not possess the advanced military technology necessary to match the ENDF [Ethiopian National Defence Forces]," he says. "It has lost many of its generals, strategic thinkers, finest diplomats and fighters, either through defections or arrests. The infighting within the TPLF leadership has caused significant damage."
Abraha Hailezgi, a scholar at Mekelle University, agrees. "The army lacks a clear political vision. In recent years, it has become associated with coercion, abuses, forced recruitment and arbitrary actions. As a result, many people have come to view the TPLF army as an adversary rather than a force acting on their behalf," he says.
Speaking by telephone from an undisclosed location, TPLF spokesperson Mikael Asgedom denies that the group has lost.
Instead, he describes it as a deliberate tactical and strategic retreat. "This is not a defeat," he tells the BBC.
Dozens of people were killed in drone strikes during the short conflict
He says the TPLF "intentionally allowed the ENDF to advance deeper into the heartland of Tigray", where it can be isolated and confronted on favourable terrain. "We chose not to fight on terms favourable to the enemy."
The TPLF is preparing for a major counteroffensive, he says, adding that TPLF fighters have launched attacks against Ethiopian forces in several locations following their withdrawal from the region's towns, arguing that these operations demonstrated the group's continued military capability.
It is hard to get verified information from Tigray and the BBC is unable to report from there. But phone lines and the internet, which were cut when fighting broke out, have now been restored.
Residents in different parts of Tigray tell the BBC that fighting is continuing in central, northern and north-western parts of Tigray, with the use of heavy artillery and drone strikes.
Eyewitnesses around Sheraro, a town near the Eritrean border, report heavy fighting involving artillery and ground forces in recent days.
"We could hear heavy artillery fire from the Sheraro direction. People are concerned because there is no sense of security," a businessman tells the BBC on condition of anonymity. He adds that military convoys from both sides had moved towards Sheraro, while a motorcycle operator in the southern town of Yechila says military checkpoints are still active.
Memories of the devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war remain raw for many residents.
The conflict saw widespread human rights abuses and allegations of ethnic cleansing in Western Tigray, while estimates suggest the war claimed hundreds of thousands of lives.
As soldiers from Eritrea, accused of some of the worst atrocities in the previous conflict, and Ethiopia have reappeared in Tigray's towns, many residents describe a profound sense of fear and anxiety, saying the sight of the troops has reopened still-fresh wounds.
Military sources aligned with the federal army say operations against the TPLF are continuing, with recent fighting and troop movements reported in northern Tigray, near the Eritrean border, as well as across central Tigray's rugged highlands. They claim the TPLF's capabilities are being steadily degraded.
Security analysts and observers agree that unrest is likely to continue for some time. "I see a situation in which there could be a prolonged war in Tigray," Yared Tibebu, a well-known Ethiopian commentator based in the US, tells the BBC.
Yared argues that the TPLF has a long history of waging protracted armed struggles and believes the movement is once again preparing for a lengthy conflict. He believes that once the group has reorganised its military and political structures, it may attempt to resume offensive operations.
However he believes this will not happen for some time because of internal divisions - a suggestion dismissed by TPLF spokesperson Mikael.
The army says it seized all these weapons from the TPLF during the fighting
Hudson rejects the idea that Tigray is heading towards a prolonged war but agrees that the region may not be truly peaceful for some time. "The TPLF may continue a low-level insurgency and guerrilla campaign, but that is not war. I do not think there will be a wider-scale conflict between the federal forces and the TPLF."
He says the TPLF no longer possesses the size, strength or military capability required to effectively confront federal forces, which he says have significantly expanded and modernised in recent years. "The TPLF has also lost much of its public support and cannot easily rebuild its ranks through recruitment," he says.
Yared, on the other hand, points to the TPLF's history of overcoming setbacks as evidence that the movement could recover to sustain a prolonged struggle. "The TPLF has overcome many major challenges in the past. It is wrong to conclude that it has no public support. It is a political movement with a history stretching back more than 50 years," he says.
Most Mekelle residents only have money for the basic necessities at the moment
What Yared sees as a strength, Hudson sees as a weakness, saying the TPLF is still "trapped in the past", and continues to behave as a dominant party within Tigray, even though the situation has changed. "It is a movement that has not evolved, modernised or expanded."
While Hudson argues that the TPLF is not equipped to sustain a major military campaign, the TPLF spokesman says the group obtains weapons and logistical supplies from the Ethiopian military. "We seize weapons from our enemy, and the weaponry that has entered Tigray will, sooner or later, become ours."
In early October, eyewitnesses told the BBCthey had seen Eritrean troops in Tigray amid reports they were backing the TPLF.  However, they appear to have returned home and Hudson thinks the country would be wary of becoming further embroiled in the conflict.
"First, Eritrea does not have unlimited resources. Second, the TPLF is no more an effective military force, and Eritrean leaders may have concluded that supporting it at this stage would not yield significant military gains," he says. "Third, Eritrea would have to consider the risk of provoking a confrontation with Ethiopia if it openly backs the TPLF."
Sources in the Ethiopia army tell the BBC that senior members of the TPLF's political leadership were briefly based in Eritrea, however, they say the authorities ordered them to leave in early November, shortly after President Isaias Afwerki returned from Russia. According to the sources, the move was driven by concerns that Ethiopia could use their presence as a reason to invade.
Hudson also argues that Eritrea's renewed diplomatic engagement with the US, whose relations with the TPLF have long been strained, could further discourage Asmara from providing meaningful support to the movement.
In September, seven Ethiopian rebel groups led by the TPLF announced the formation of a new coalition called the Alliance for Survival, aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government.
Seven rebel groups from across Ethiopia have announced a new alliance
Yared believes the alliance could give the TPLF the strength to keep on fighting. "Its members can combine their strengths. The TDF [the TPLF's military wing] has leadership experience and organisational capacity, while Fano [an ethnic Amhara militia] is believed to have between 70,000 and 80,000 fighters.
"If conditions emerge that allow the forces to co-ordinate effectively, the TPLF's current difficulties may not last long," he says.
Hudson, however, rejects that argument, insisting that the alliance is unlikely to alter the balance of power. "I don't think the TPLF can be saved by this alliance. The ethnic militias have not demonstrated the capacity, either individually or collectively, to pose a serious threat to federal forces. We should not underestimate the strength of the federal army," he says.

title: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone in Gulf of Finland
summary: The attack is thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an open stretch of the Baltic Sea.
body:
The Naro-Fominsk is believed to have headed back to port in St Petersburg after the attack
Finnish officials have confirmed that a Russian warship was attacked in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, although little is known about the strike.
Ukraine's SBU security service said it targeted the ship Naro-Fominsk as part of a broader drone operation against Russia's Ust-Luga oil export depot on the Baltic coast.
The attack, thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic Sea open to civilian maritime traffic, has raised questions about whether Ukraine could expand its strikes.
Helsinki has been one of Kyiv's closest European allies, and Finnish officials have described the incident as a direct result of Russia's continued full-scale war.
Finland's military has given few details of the incident, but it appears to have taken place in a narrow stretch some distance from the Finnish coast.
The country's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen was adamant that the situation in the Baltic Sea remained stable and safe and that there was no threat of any kind to marine traffic.
Defence officials are understood to have stressed to Kyiv that the Gulf is a relatively narrow waterway used by oil tankers and civilian vessels, and is also home to subsea data cables.
Ukraine's SBU described the Russian ship as a Buyan-M type small corvette that carried Kalibr and Oniks cruise missiles. There were also unconfirmed reports of Russian combat helicopters being destroyed.
Martin Herem, the defence minister of Estonia, which borders the Gulf, told public broadcaster ERR that the ship was hit at about 05:30 (03:30 GMT) on Wednesday but did not say how it was attacked: "We know that smoke came from the ship afterwards. The ship itself went back towards St Petersburg."
The extent of casualties or damage sustained by the Russian navy ship remains unclear, and Moscow rarely gives such details.
"The Baltic Sea fleet has been untouched up to this point but there seemingly was a window of opportunity for Ukraine and they understandably tried to use it," said military analyst Emil Kastehelmi, co-founder of the Black Bird monitoring group.
Russian and Ukrainian vessels have been repeatedly targeted in the Black Sea since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, but even though the latest strike on a ship in the Baltic is unprecedented, Kastehelmi told the BBC he did not consider it a serious escalation.
Ukrainian drones are regularly launched into Russia from northern Ukraine. Several storage tanks at the Ust-Luga terminal are thought to have been hit overnight on Wednesday and fires at the port were visible over the border in Estonia.
Herem said Ukrainian drones attacked the Ust-Luga region from midnight until about 06:00, mostly flying close to the Estonian border but still in Russian airspace.
He added that one drone had entered Estonian airspace briefly from Latvia and then headed towards Russia.
Nato aircraft based in the Baltic states were in the air at the time, but Herem said it had not been considered safe for them to destroy the drones.
Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesman Heorhiy Tykhyy said late on Wednesday that Moscow's allegations that Kyiv had used the airspace of the Baltic states to attack Russia were "baseless", although he acknowledged "incidents might occur when Russia diverts drones from its airspace using electronic warfare".

title: Suspected bomb hoax threats force fresh evacuations of Italian schools
summary: Schools across Italy have received bomb threats for the second day in a row, sparking fresh panic and evacuations.
body:
Bomb squads have searched many schools but no devices have been found
Schools across Italy have received bomb threats for the second day in a row, sparking fresh panic and evacuations.
Some 3,778 schools, from Milan in the north to Sicily in the south, reported similar threats to one that created chaos on Wednesday - even though no explosive devices have been found.
The government has advised schools that "in the absence of concrete evidence beyond the simple receipt of a mass email indicating a danger, buildings must not not be evacuated". Unlike a day earlier, only 77 schools were evacuated on Thursday, authorities say.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni says her government will come up with "sector-specific" advice to help those facing this kind of threat.
Schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland received threats on Wednesday, too. It is unclear whether the incidents are connected.
On Thursday morning, a bomb alert at a Calais rail station delayed international and national train services in northern France.
The latest incidents follow a series of bomb hoaxes last week against airports and airlines in a number of European countries.
Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.
Wednesday's email threat - sent to 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 Italian state schools   - was said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan".
Some officials say it originated in Taiwan.
A similar message sent to Italian schools on Thursday, again signed by Mikhail Andropov, is said to have been sent from the account of a teacher in the Philippines whose account is believed to have been hacked.
No risk to public from hoax school bomb threats, says government minister
Police treating threatening email sent to more than 300 schools as 'hoax'
Many parents, though, are concerned and have been demanding clarity and action from the government.
La Repubblica newspaper reports that protests have been held against a decision by the headmaster of a secondary school in Rome who did not take any action, saying she had realised the threatening message to contain typos and therefore be "fake".
According to the newspaper, protesters want new national guidelines to be issued.

title: Microsoft struggling to restore service as global outage affects Outlook and Teams
summary: Microsoft said the outage was caused by servers unexpected becoming unavailable, straining other systems.
body:
Microsoft is struggling to fix a major global outageof its service that is reportedly affecting tens of thousands of users.
Services including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot have been affected by "connectivity problems".
"We're aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact," thecompany wrote on X.
Reports of problems with Outlook peaked globally at nearly 140,000 around 18:00 GMT on Thursday, according to monitoring website Downdetector.
The BBC understands there is no indication the outage was caused by a cyber-attack.
The disruption affects programs that are part of Microsoft 365 - a popular online service among businesses that allows them to use workplace tools like Outlook, Teams and OneDrive.
For international organisations, this platform is essential for connecting and collaborating with colleagues around the world.
Among the issues, users may be unable to view certain files or details on their calendar apps, Microsoft said.
Its AI platform, Copilot, may also be unable to work properly.
Messaging and online meetings were largely functional, the firm added.
Microsoft said on X that the outage was caused by a number of servers "being unexpectedly unavailable", straining its remaining systems.
The company is working to address the issues with its services, said a Microsoft spokesperson.
"We appreciate our customers' patience while we work to restore services as soon as possible."
The company later warned that some services that had been restored "can become unresponsive again", adding that customers "in any region" could be affected.
Users around the world including the US, Japan and Singapore have reported facing disruptions.
The outage has hit other companies, including AI giants Anthropic and OpenAI, which work with Microsoft's systems.
ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which has caused some tools to not work as expected.
Microsoft last month reported an outage of its Azure cloud platform that affected the tech giant's suite of productivity tools and companies worldwide.
Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on 12 November, rescheduled it to 16 November, citing business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outage.

title: The rise of 'housefishing' - when does using AI go from enhancing to misleading?
summary: Experts warn that using AI to enhance property images can go too far and mislead prospective buyers.
body:
The images Olivia Nicole saw of a home on Rightmove (l) were completely different to how the property looked in real life (r)
Have you ever been impressed by the pictures of a property on an estate agent's website, only to find the place looks completely different when you view it in person?
Then there's a chance that AI was used to enhance the images you saw.
From repainted walls to imaginary lawns, estate agents are increasingly using the technology to make homes seem more appealing, arguing it helps buyers visualise the potential of a place.
But experts warn it can go too far and mislead prospective buyers - a trend dubbed "housefishing".
So how much AI enhancement is too much?
Earlier this year Olivia Nicole, 29, was searching online for five-bedroom properties in south-west London when a house on Rightmove caught her eye.
But when she arrived to view it several days later she initially thought she had come to the wrong place.
"The rooms were much smaller than they were in the pictures and the decor was totally different," she tells the BBC. "Some structural features were also different."
For example, there was a raised section of the wall behind the sofa that didn't appear in the images. The windows were also noticeably smaller. Olivia was so surprised she took her own pictures of the property for comparison.
AI has been used to make the property look more luxurious
It later turned out the pictures she had seen on Rightmove, which also appeared on the Zoopla and Winkworth websites, were enhanced with AI.
But that wasn't clear in the listing, Olivia says, and she feels the agent wasted her time.
"It was frustrating, because I had taken several hours off work for the viewing which I had to make up for."
All three companies told the BBC they had strict guidelines on how AI could be used on their websites and have since taken the images down.
Estate agents have long used wide-angle lens cameras or Photoshop to make homes seem bigger or more appealing to buyers, but AI is making this process much easier and more accessible.
It is difficult to quantify how common the practice is, says the Guild of Property Professionals, a trade group of independent estate agents, but it has issued guidance on how to use AI enhancement responsibly.
According to a recent survey,externalof 906 UK homebuyers, one in five who had who purchased a home in the past year said they had viewed a property where the listing photos had been digitally enhanced to make the home appear better than it actually was.
Jack Bushrod reviews quirky property listings he finds on Rightmove for his social media channel, Housing Horrors, and says he has seen a "surge" of AI-enhanced images over the last six months.
He thinks using AI is fine up to a point - to declutter a busy room, or add furniture to an empty one so a prospective buyer can see its potential.
But he draws the line at anything that misleads a prospective buyer or wastes their time.
"I've seen one house where they had removed a pillar and added a window. Others might use AI to remove stains on the carpet or cracks in tiles. It's little details you would only notice in person."
He says most of the enhanced images he's seen weren't clearly labelled as AI-generated.
Cara says AI was used to empty her son's room in the image on the left
Cara, 38, is currently selling her home in Lowestoft, Suffolk, and says she was surprised when she saw the AI-enhanced pictures of her property her estate agent, Howards, put on Rightmove.
In one photo, her son's room was completely emptied of toys and clutter.
In another, of her daughter's room, the agent appears to have removed a doll's house, brightened the room, and used AI to change the shape of a rug, but that image has since been taken down.
Cara has had several viewings so far and says that one person has commented on the differences. But she says she trusts Howards, which has acknowledged the use of AI in the property listing.
"If they'd changed something structurally or it was really wild and didn't look like our home at all then I would put my foot down," she says.
In one picture (l), the AI removed a doll's house and changed the shape of a rug
A spokeswoman told the BBC that Howards had now introduced a policy of labelling all AI-enhanced photos. She added that the firm never used AI "to misrepresent the fundamental features of a property".
"It's about helping people imagine the possibilities, not changing the reality of what's being sold."
Trading Standards told the BBC that estate agents can use AI to make basic enhancements to photos, or to virtually furnish an empty room or garden, as long as they indicate they have used the technology.
But it says structurally changing a room, for example by adding a window, or hiding features could mislead consumers and break the law.
Jack Bushrod thinks all estate agents should have to clearly label AI-enhanced photos and mention any use of the tech prominently in the key features slide of a property listing.
He also expects to see more housefishing as time goes on.
"My worry is the more estate agents use AI, others will see the trend and jump on the bandwagon."

title: Who is Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress - and who could take over permanently?
summary: Chief financial officer Colette Kress in in charge of Nvidia for now, but several others are in the frame as potential successors.
body:
Arm's boss Rene Haas (L), Nvidia's Colette Kress (C) and Chris Malachowsky (R) have been named as possible successors
Nvidia is now facing a scenario few would have considered until very recently - a future without Jensen Huang.
The influential co-founder of the AI chip-making giant resigned on Thursday over reports of extramarital affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Chief financial officer Colette Kress is in charge, for now, as the tech giant faces one of its biggest challenges - finding the right person to permanently lead the business that Huang helped create more than three decades ago and turned into one of the world's most valuable companies.
We take a look at which candidates have emerged as potential successors.
Colette Kress is chief financial officer at Nvidia
Colette Kress has been an industry veteran for more than 30 years, having previously held high positions at tech firms like Cisco and Microsoft.
Kress, who also serves as Nvidia's executive vice-president, has seen the firm's transformation from making chips for video games in the early 1990s to becoming an AI semiconductor powerhouse.
She has "fronted every earnings call" alongside Huang and is a "familiar and trusted voice for the market at a time when it badly needs one," said Josh Gilbert, an analyst at investment firm eToro.
But doing the job permanently could be a different story, said Gilbert, as the firm, known for its edge in technology, could want an engineer in the chair.
Chris Malachowsky is one of Nvidia's three co-founders
Another option is Chris Malachowsky, who founded Nvidia alongside Huang and Curtis Priem, and is the only executive that shares the same level of seniority.
Malachowsky has played a key part in developing the company's computing technology.
Ian Buck, who oversees Nvidia's high-performance computing business, has also emerged as a potential candidate if the company is keen to put an engineer in the top job.
Buck was among the early pioneers who helped popularise the use of graphic processors beyond gaming applications.
"He could protect Nvidia's technological edge, but his ability to manage the wider commercial relationships and geopolitical challenges would face scrutiny," said Charu Chanana, investment strategist at investment bank Saxo.
Today, Nvidia's leading processors are widely regarded as the gold standard for AI development.
Huang's children also work at Nvidia in executive positions but are relatively young and inexperienced.
Nvidia is likely to favour an internal appointment initially but could look externally for a more permanent replacement, said Jun Bei Liu, founder and lead portfolio manager at Ten Cap.
Several names of tech entrepreneurs outside of Nvidia have been floated by experts.
Liu said Apple's former chief executive, Tim Cook, could be a possible choice as someone familiar with managing global supply chains, though she questioned whether he would be willing to leave the iPhone maker, where he is the chair.
Apple's Tim Cook (R) with Jensen Huang (L) and his wife Lori Huang at the White House
Liu and Chanana also suggested Rene Haas, chief executive of Arm Holdings, the UK chipmaking giant.
Nvidia's processors are made with the help of chipmakers around the world, including Taiwan's TSMC and South Korea's SK Hynix and Samsung.
Rene Haas is the boss of Arm Holdings
Haas is familiar with leading a publicly-listed company and would bring semiconductor experience, though Nvidia's business model is considerably different from Arm's, said Chanana.
"The challenge is finding someone who can combine Jensen's technical understanding, strategic vision and relationships across the global technology industry," Liu said.
Ten Cap's Liu had believed it was just a matter of time before Huang would step down as Nvidia's chief executive.
"The issue is no longer simply about personal conduct," she said. "It is about corporate governance, national security concerns and maintaining confidence in the leadership of one of the world's most strategically important companies."
Several major investment firms have downgraded their forecasts for the chip giant - a rare shift given investors' longstanding optimism about the company.
An early indication came as markets opened in New York shortly after Huang's resignation was announced.
Nvidia shares opened down more than 13%, wiping more than half a trillion dollars off the firm's share market value.
Jensen Huang's departure leaves a void in the influential AI giant
Stacy Rasgon, senior analyst in US semiconductors at Bernstein Research, wrote in a note to investors that "our gut tells us we probably haven't fully probed the depths of what might be found here".
Rasgon halved Bernstein's share price target for Nvidia and said: "We've had enough and prefer to watch from the sidelines."
Ray Wang, chief executive of Constellation Research, said the crisis isn't so much an issue for the wider AI industry but rather one for Nvidia itself which has to consider if the person it appoints as its chief executive has the same appeal as Huang.
"That's really what the issue is, because a lot of these partnerships and investments have been made because of the trust with with Jensen," he said.

title: Faisal Islam: Why the UK economy is surprisingly resilient
summary: The UK is seeing impressive growth, but will it last?
body:
The UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in the three months to September.
"Top gear" and "strikingly strong" were among the descriptions of the 0.7% growth  offered by the economists who track every minor murmur of Britain's economy.
It is an upgrade on "solid" and "resilient", and in turn a world away from "hardest hit by the Iran War".
Against the backdrop of the world's biggest disruption to energy flows, rising market borrowing costs - and the cruel summers since the pandemic -it is impressive growth.
It should reset some of the swirl of self-reinforcing negativity.
The UK's economic growth has averaged less than 0.1% in the four Q3s [ie July to September] since the pandemic.
The average prediction just months ago for this July to September was just 0.1%.
Even the UK's official forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) effectively pencilled in 0.3% at the Budget just 3 weeks ago.
This figure has not been exceeded outside the pandemic since 2017. It puts the UK on course to be the second fastest growing economy after the US across the major G7 countries  which also includes Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France.
It is tempting to think about what the economy would have done if the Iran War hadn't happened. If interest rates had been cut instead of their recent rise.
While the latest figure kills the doom, it is clearly not a boom either.
Spending on AI and tech have driven the surprise upside over the year. While the AI data centre boom may at any point turn to bust, these figures suggest that spending across the economy on investing in these technologies is helping to boost  growth. Consumers have been resilient, at least till the autumn, perhaps helped by better economic vibes.
While there has been an understandable focus on high UK borrowing costs, another measure of the international standing of the UK economy, sterling's value, reached post Brexit referendum highs last week.
Productivity and investment is also looking stronger, especially after recent revisions. Some of the most encouraging figures are in private sector business investment.
I spoke to the chancellor at Nexeon in Oxfordshire, which is searching for a UK factory to manufacture its cutting edge electric vehicle battery - and British - technology. My colleagues visited British watchmakers in Maidenhead carving out a niche to take on the Swiss.
However, this may well not last for the final three months of the year.
Consumer confidence has already fallen as petrol and domestic energy prices start to rise again.
There is a significant challenge with everyday cost-of-living pressures in the coming months. Construction and private house building remain depressed.
The Iran conflict remains the big unknown and whether post the US midterm elections there could be a durable end to the conflict in the Gulf.
Some oil and gas production there is starting to normalise. It could bring down petrol prices, energy bills, government borrowing costs, and mortgage costs too.
Expect to see Downing Street investing heavily in "settlement of the conflict", which the chancellor told me is the "best economic policy".

title: Some under-25s should get fewer benefits, Milburn review to say
summary: The proposed radical overhaul of the welfare system would move under-25s off the main sickness benefits.
body:
Alan Milburn will publish his review next week
Some young people could see reductions to the benefits they are entitled to under a radical overhaul of the welfare system to be recommended by a government-commissioned review.
As reported in the Times,,externalAlan Milburn's year-long report, to be published on Tuesday, is expected to recommend moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits.
Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, has been tasked by the government with helping reduce the one in eight 16 to 24 year-olds in the UK who are not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet".
He said on Wednesday night that his plans would not be "pain-free" and would affect both existing and new claimants.
His report is expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wideuniversal credit- orpersonal independence payment(Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales.
Disabled people in Scotland can claim the devolved Adult Disability Payment.
Instead, under Milburn's plan, under-25s would receive an allowance on the same basic rate as universal credit.
Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to their conditions.
Some claimants would receive less under the plans - although the exact amounts will not be clear until early next year, when the government publishes legislation to implement the changes.
People can claim Pip to help them with the additional cost of being disabled or living with long-term physical or mental health conditions. It is available to those both in and out of work.
In his interim report,,externalMilburn said survey data found that 19% of young people claiming disability or health benefits were in work.
Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, is also expected to recommend an investment of billions into more employment support for young people, including work placements, job subsidies and one-to-one personal advisers.
Those with more severe disabilities and unable to work would get a new benefit paid at a higher rate.
Milburn told the Times: "Candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system.
"But actually, for young people, there's a different debate that we've got to resolve, which is whether the priority is their longer-term life chances or just their immediate shorter-term finances.
"I think what the current system does [is] it prioritises the latter over the former. I believe that's the wrong choice and it needs to be the other way around."
Speaking later on Thursday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said young people would be given support "when they need it as teenagers rather than leaving them on benefits in their 20s".
He added: "The principle that we will be working on is that we will guarantee support for young people and that is the whole basis on which we will proceed."
Just under one million young people in the UK are Neets, data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) from April to June suggests. This was a rise of 3% on the same period last year.
Milburn's recommendations are likely to be backed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham but could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who opposed welfare changes last year under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.
Dame Meg Hillier, who helped spearhead a backbench rebellion against Starmer's reforms, suggested she and her colleagues were broadly supportive this time around.
"What happened last year was a cut was being proposed and none of us could explain to people what would happen to them," the Labour MP told the BBC.
"Milburn has done some very good work on this so I'm giving him a fair wind," she added.
But Bell Ribeiro-Addy, one of the Labour backbenchers who revolted last year, said she was "not sure" she could vote to cut the benefit entitlement of existing claimants.
Tom Ashforth, a 19-year-old student at Sheffield Hallam University, receives both components of Pip at the higher rate.
He said the financial support helps him manage additional expenses linked to his visual impairment, including prescriptions, mobility aids and accessible learning resources.
"If I were to lose it, I would struggle to afford essential things," he said.
Student Tom said he relies on the money he gets from Pip to support him through his time at university
He said he believes decisions over disability benefits should be made on a case-by-case basis, rather than according to age.
"You cannot assume that everyone under the age of 25 is in the same position," he said.
In his Times interview, Milburn acknowledged that changing the rules for existing claimants would be "difficult politically" but stressed it was necessary.
James Taylor, from disability equality charity Scope, said Pip was a "lifeline" and restricting access to it "won't make young disabled people's extra costs disappear".
Harriet Edwards, from the charity Sense, said changes were "long overdue", but that without additional details, families were "deeply anxious".
A government spokesperson said: "We will always ensure there is a safety net for the most vulnerable and those who are unable to work."
The reforms would represent a radical overhaul of Britain's welfare system, at a time when there is heavy political pressure for the UK to find the money to spend more on defence.
Both the Conservatives and Reform UK have argued for significant cuts to welfare, including to fund a boost to defence.
Responding on Thursday, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the government should not be spending "lots of time" on employment schemes, which she said would ultimately fail.
If Milburn's recommendations were approved, it could take almost a decade for the British state to see monetary savings.
The new system "will need significant investment" and would involve "rebuilding the system from scratch", Milburn said.
His new proposed system would involve an element of carrot and stick, wherein young people could lose some of their benefits if they did not engage with the extra work support options.
In an interview recorded on Tuesday, Skills Minister Jacqui Smith told the BBC that young people had a "responsibility" to take up employment support.
"It is a contract. People need the chance, and they need to take that chance," she added.
A separate review - co-chaired by disabilities minister Sir Stephen Timms - examining disability benefits is also expected to be published this month.

title: Can Burnham avoid another Labour welfare rebellion?
summary: Any revolt among MPs is likely to be smaller than the one that badly damaged Keir Starmer's government.
body:
A review by Alan Milburn (left) could create political headaches for Andy Burnham
Andy Burnham has committed to bringing the welfare bill down, but he knows just how the high the political stakes are.
He saw how last year's welfare rebellion marked the beginning of the end for his predecessor in Downing Street.
Sir Keir Starmer's authority was shredded when 120 - more than a quarter - of his own MPs threatened to derail his reforms.
To defuse this, Sir Keir was compelled to guarantee that existing claimants of personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales, wouldn't lose out.
Even then, 49 of the 120 potential Labour rebels still voted against their own government.
Next week, a review from former New Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn has the capacity to create another internal row in Labour's ranks.
Milburn has spent a year grappling with how to reduce the nearly one million young people who are not in employment, education or training (Neets).
In an interview with the Times, he has now confirmed he is set to recommend cutting benefits for some 16-24 year olds who currently receive Pip, or the enhanced health-related payment of Universal Credit.
Taking benefit cuts to the Parliamentary Labour Party would usually have a similar effect to adding phosphorous to water.
But from my soundings, the deep waters of the Labour ranks are calmer than might be expected.
Importantly, two of the most effective organisers of last year's welfare rebellion are batting for the current prime minister, rather than against the previous one.
Louise Haigh is now the most powerful cabinet minister after Andy Burnham himself, while Anneliese Midgeley is his chief whip.
And the MP who fronted that rebellion - Meg Hillier - has said she wants to give Milburn's proposals a "fair wind".
There are also clear differences to the previous approach to welfare reform.
First, it is not being presented as primarily a cost-cutting exercise with pre-determined savings.
Instead, there will be upfront investment to provide more support to unemployed young people, and a timeframe for net savings likely to be set at around a decade – gradualism, not a short, sharp shock.
Second, last year's initial reforms would have affected people in all age groups, whilst benefit cuts this time would be limited to the under 25s, who make up around 11% of Pip claimants.
Some under-25s should get fewer benefits, Milburn review to say
One in eight young people still out of work or education ahead of major review
I've spoken to government ministers who had expressed concerns – at least privately – about the changes devised previously by Rachel Reeves and Liz Kendall.  This time, they are on board.
One of them told me that so long as there was enough support for young people, with guaranteed jobs and training, MPs would be "fine" with some benefit cuts.
But they added that it was vital that those who really couldn't work wouldn't be worse off.
Milburn will suggest there could even be enhanced payments for people in this category, while some young people with disabilities who lose out on Pip could nonetheless be given an additional "allowance" to help with living costs.
Another minister who opposed the previous reforms praised the process this time.
There had been a high level of engagement not just from Milburn, but Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden, who has been taking MPs through the principles behind the reforms.
One minister was a little more cautious, suggesting support for a reduction in benefits would depend on what the entire "package" of reforms looked like.
Milburn's recommendations are likely to be wide-ranging – from pre-school policies to how the NHS deals with mental health.
Some of the eventual 49 rebels from last year are in a similar place.
York MP Rachael Maskell told me it was essential that she saw the detail of the proposals rather than the "drip, drip" of press reports which would "cause young people stress and distress".
She felt withdrawing Pip from young people was "like a sledgehammer to crack a nut" and was concerned that some disabled people required it to remain in work.
She also suggested that the government "shouldn't just point the finger at young people," and should look closely at how employers could take more youngsters on.
Stroud MP Simon Opher also voted against the government on welfare last year.
He told me there was a "crisis" with so many Neets, and Milburn had come up with a "credible solution".
But he believes cutting benefits should be a "last resort" and is worried about restricting access to the health element of Universal Credit, as a quarter of young claimants aren't Neet. He concludes that the "devil will be in the detail".
So much of politics - like comedy – depends on timing.
For some sceptics, including serving ministers, the Milburn proposals will be more warmly welcomed if support for young people is in place before entitlements are withdrawn.
But for some Labour MPs, cutting payments to existing claimants crosses a line.
Clapham and Brixton Hill MP Bell Ribiero-Addy has she wasn't sure she could back cuts.
Referring to Pip, she didn't believe that "you get a disabled young person into work by taking away the money that helps them to get into work".
And another MP on the left of the party, Brian Leishman, told the BBC he couldn't back benefits cuts as "we are in the middle of a cost of living crisis".
So a welfare rebellion seems guaranteed if Burnham accepts Milburn's recommendations.
But it seems unlikely to be of the same scale, or have a similar level of political jeopardy to the one which shook the Starmer government.

title: Military base asylum plans granted planning approval
summary: The Home Office's application to house up to 1,256 men at the site near Bicester was fast-tracked.
body:
The government plans are for accommodating up to 1,256 men at the site near Bicester
Planning permission to house asylum seekers at a former military site near the Oxfordshire village of Piddington has been granted by the government.
The Home Office's applicationto house up to 1,256 menat the MoD Bicester site was fast-tracked using an Urgent Crown Development application.
The nearby village of Piddington symbolically voted to leave the UK in opposition to the planned site, which has also beenlegally challengedby campaigners.
A Home Office spokesperson said the planning permission "allows us to continue to progress the use of MoD Bicester" but no final decision on the proposal had been taken.
A government report said the decision received 3,177 representations against, and one in support.
It also said Housing Secretary Angela Rayner ruled permission should be granted because "national demand for asylum accommodation remains high".
The permission allows for demolition of existing buildings, the erection of new modular accommodation, and provisions for health and welfare facilities.
Chris Philp MP, Shadow Home Secretary, said: "Angela Rayner and the Labour government have betrayed the people of Piddington by abusing their emergency powers in this way."
He continued: "Instead of accommodating illegal immigrants, the government should leave the ECHR so they can be rapidly deported."
The decision was made despite campaigners lodging their complaints to the High Court
Lib Dem MP for Bicester and Woodstock Calum Miller said it was "the wrong plan and the wrong site for local communities, asylum seekers and taxpayers".
"I am deeply disappointed that the government has approved this proposal despite the serious concerns raised by residents and local councils as well as the major problems with the site," he added.
The approval could be challenged by an application to the High Court within six weeks, beginning with the day after the date of the decision.
The government said a challenge "may be brought only on the ground that the decision is legally flawed; it is not an opportunity to reconsider the planning merits".
Joe Marshall, a Piddington parish councillor, said residents of the village were "extremely frustrated".
"The government has approved its own application against more than 3,000 objections and one letter of support, overruling the councils, the NHS and the Police and Crime Commissioner," he said.
"No wonder we voted to leave the UK."
He told BBC Newsnight: "This development is something that nobody would want to have imposed on their local area."
Villagers voted overwhelmingly to become an independent state in a symbolic referendum
Reform UK home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said: "Over 1,200 unvetted illegal migrant men are being dumped in Piddington.
"Tory and Labour governments have betrayed their own people. Reform will detain and deport all of these men."
A Home Office spokesperson said: "A final decision to proceed is yet to be taken.
"The government is working on a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country, with over £1 billion saved in costs since the election.
"This includes closing all asylum hotels and moving to alternative accommodation, including former military sites.
"These are designed to be self-contained, with 24/7 security and CCTV, to minimise the impact on the local community."

title: Burnham's push for closer EU ties causes ripples in his party and others
summary: Ahead of a week which will focus minds on the UK's relationship with the bloc, the prime minister's stance on Europe is causing MPs to think about their leaders' individual strategy.
body:
There is renewed attention on the prime minister's push for closer relations with Europe - and that is causing ripples in his own party and others.
Andy Burnham told his Cabinet earlier this week: "I firmly believe we have ended up with a harder Brexit than people voted for… no sensible person thinks the deal negotiated by the Tories is working for the country."
It comes ahead of a week which will focus minds on the UK's relationship with the bloc. On Thursday, at a gathering of European leaders in Dublin, Burnham will for the first time meet those who could prove pivotal as he sells his vision for Britain's future in the bloc.
And next week, he will deliver a speech on foreign policy, in which – for Burnham – Europe is a central plank. He will then travel to Brussels for a UK-EU summit to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility.
Talking about the new deal to be signed at the summit, Burnham said to ministers: "We will take opportunities that make people in this country better off.
"There is a significant prize."
Brexit referendum 'possible' in Labour election manifesto, says Burnham
UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports
This lies behind the prime minister's decision to open the door to the argument about rejoining the EU single market - along with the freedom of movement that would bring - and even the EU altogether.
But that longer-term ambition is dividing his cabinet and his party.
Some welcome his approach, including those with formerly Brexit-backing constituencies. Angela Rayner, for example, is understood to have been pushing former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer to be bolder on Brexit since at least autumn 2022.
The housing secretary is said to have been insistent that Labour needs to stick to its manifesto red lines – not to return to the EU single market, customs union, or freedom of movement – but is open minded to changing those at the next election.
Another cabinet minister said: "The best thing you can do in politics is tell the truth. And the truth is that Brexit has been hugely damaging to Britain.
"We are not leading a public conversation here, we are racing to catch up with the public."
But others are watching nervously at a strategy one former minister described as "high risk".
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, for example, has struck a more cautious tone warning about the "costs and consequences" of rejoining the EU as well as staying out.
Jonathan Reynolds, the Business and Trade Secretary, is supportive of getting closer to the EU and discussing the UK's long term relationship.
But he has previously warned against joining the EU's customs union and is also unsure about the prospect of rejoining the EU, highlighting the uncertainty of what terms the UK would face, and what the bloc could look like in years to come with nationalist parties in the ascendancy in several European countries.
A voice from the past has a different set of concerns.
Lord Cameron told Bloomberg's Mishal Husain that starting a conversation about rejoining would be "very long and painful".
The former prime minister warned "flirting with rejoining" could also harm Burnham's attempts to renegotiate the Conservative's Brexit deal.
"If you start endlessly producing this idea that we're actually on a path to rejoining, I think you're in danger of getting a less good partnership deal because of course the EU countries will just think: 'Well, these guys are gonna rejoin anyway, so what's the point in giving them a good partnership deal'."
Attitudes in Labour towards the prime minister's approach don't divide along predictable lines. One Scottish Labour MP, personally opposed to Brexit and with a heavily Remain-voting constituency, said it was a "real problem".
"How can I argue to my constituents that we had a Scottish referendum in 2014 that settled independence for a generation. but then say the 2016 referendum isn't settled? My view is you accept democracy."
For now though, that opposition hasn't broken out into public rebellion, although Labour MP Gareth Snell is one who has warned about reopening the debate.
The MP for Stoke-on-Trent, where the Leave vote was 69.4%, told the BBC's Westminster Hour that doing so would "monopolise an awful lot of time inside parliament, inside government" when there are other things MPs should be doing.
Two Labour MPs among those most unhappy about Burnham's openness to Europe insisted "there are no plans" for any organised criticism of the prime minister.
Despite their concerns, particularly about free movement, they described their current mindset as "wait and see". That temporary truce is likely to fracture if the prime minister's lead in the polls begins to slide.
Badenoch has pledged that a future Conservative government will withdraw the UK from the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR)
But Burnham's strategy has left other parties struggling to react.
The Conservatives have strongly opposed any move to align with EU rules into the future, with the party leader Kemi Badenoch saying that would be a red line and "actually take us backwards".
But some Conservative MPs are beginning to express unease about the strategic dilemma presented for their party by Burnham's moves on Europe, fearing that the issue could again divide Conservative voters.
In recent months Badenoch and her team have intensified efforts to win back affluent voters, especially in the south of England, who view Burnham's economic offer as too left-wing.
"The problem is that some of those voters are only just giving us a hearing again after Brexit," one Conservative MP said, "and now they are going to keep being reminded of it."
The Liberal Democrats have enjoyed being the most pro-European of the largest parties in Westminster. But some Lib Dems now fear their distinct position risks being drowned out by Burnham.
Reform UK though say they are "very bullish" about the return of Brexit to political debate, despite polling that suggests public sentiment has shifted since 2016.
"If he [Burnham] wants to fight an election on a £40bn bill to rejoin, open door immigration, and less control over our laws and our courts then we are very up for that," a Reform UK strategist said.
The party believes that just as it would build a progressive anti-Brexit coalition around Labour, it would also unite Brexit supporters around Reform UK as the most anti-EU party.

title: Some childhood offenders may no longer have to reveal convictions to employers
summary: The proposals would change how crimes committed by children are disclosed to bosses in England and Wales.
body:
Some job applicants in England and Wales would no longer need to declare criminal convictions they received as children under government proposals designed to improve the employment prospects of rehabilitated young people.
The changes would mean criminal records for people detained when they were under 18 years old would no longer show up for life during checks carried out by employers.
The Ministry of Justice has also launched a consultation on relaxing disclosure requirements for some specific drug-related and violent crimes committed by children.
Young people who have not re-offended as adults struggle to find work because of their past behaviour, the government says.
Many employers require applicants to undergo a background check, which in their most basic form require people to self-declare if they have a criminal record.
For more sensitive roles, such as working with children or joining the police, an employer can carry out a standard or enhanced check, which allows them to request information from the Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS).
How long a criminal record must be volunteered for or will show up in those checks differs depending on the severity of the offence, the punishment received and how long ago the crime was committed - sometimes referred to as whether a conviction is 'spent'.
For example, a young person who was convicted and fined for an offence when they were under-18 will have that information show up in checks for five-and-a-half years. If they were given a custodial sentence, that will be disclosed for the rest of their lives.
The government wants to reduce the number of young people those disclosure rules apply to if an applicant has not continued to offend as an adult.
Five offences would be removed from a list of crimes which will show up in background for checks for life if committed by an adult. They are: affray, violent disorder, supplying a controlled drug to a child, robbery and assaults occasioning actual bodily harm.
Between March 2022 and March 2026, around 8,500 under-18s were convicted of those offences, according to Ministry of Justice data.
The government says that type of crime is often a result of peer pressure, exploitation and "adolescent impulsivity" by individuals who are still developing, as opposed to a broader propensity for crime and violence.
Under the new rules, they would cease to show up in checks after five-and-a-half years.
Lifelong disclosure would also be removed for offences which led to a detention period of less than two years, the maximum which can be handed out by a youth court, and replaced by a new 11-year disclosure period.
In cases where a child was given a sentence longer than two years - which can only happen if the severity of the crime meant they were dealt with by an adult crown court - the rules would stay the same.
The most serious offences - including severe violence, terrorism-related crimes and sexual offences - would be exempted from the reforms.
Other proposed changes include:
Cutting or removing altogether the disclosure period for offences which led to a fine, the majority of which are for driving-related crimes
Ending disclosure of offences which were dealt with via an out of court resolution, which have primarily been used to tackle knife possession and assault
Reforming how long earlier offences appear in checks for young people who committed more than one crime as a child
Announcing a consultation on proposals, justice minister Jake Richards said: "Many young people who offend do not go on to lead lives of crime.
"They take responsibility, turn their lives around and want to make something of themselves.
"When they do, we should recognise that progress and support them – not put unnecessary barriers in their way."
The proposals come as the government prepares to publish a long-awaited report authored by former Labour minister Alan Milburn ontackling the number of young people not in work or education.
In May, he warned the UK was at risk of a raising a "lost generation" as almost one in eight young people are not working or studying.
Richards pointed to that intervention as he announced the disclosure reforms, saying barriers to employment can be "particularly difficult to overcome" for people who committed crimes as children.
